title: 'Big fat lady' hawk who ate too many chickens to fly soars free once again
summary: The red-shouldered hawk who gobbled up neighbourhood chickens until she could no longer move is slimmed down and is out on the town.

image.caption: This red-shouldered hawk was found immobilized in a driveway after eating too many neighbourhood chickens in Roanoke, Virginia. (Southwest Virginia Wildlife Center of Roanoke/Facebook)

blocks.text: As It Happens·New
The red-shouldered hawk who gobbled up neighbourhood chickens until she could no longer move is slimmed down and is out on the town.
Southwest Virginia Wildlife Center releases their star patient to much fanfare
The red-shouldered hawk who gobbled up neighbourhood chickens until she could no longer move is slimmed down and out on the town.
The Southwest Virginia Wildlife Center liberated its prodigious patient to much fanfare on Friday after downgrading her diagnosis from "too fat to fly" to just "a little over-chubby."
"We have finally released our big fat lady," Katherine McGrath, of the Southwest Virginia Wildlife Center, told As It Happens host Nil Kӧksal.
"She was definitely ready to get out of the hospital."

The hefty hawk was found belly-up last month in a driveway in Roanoke, Va. Staff at the wildlife centre ruled out injuries or illness before declaring that she had simply feasted on too many fowls to fly.
She weighed 910 grams — almost twice the average weight for her species. Meanwhile, residents reported that their free-roaming chickens had been mysteriously vanishing from their yards.
'She was crazy'

McGrath says staff put the big bird on a diet of 20 grams of mouse or rat per day, paired with "prescribed exercise where we would literally just follow her around a pen to force her to fly back and forth."
Over the course of about a month of birdy bootcamp, the hawk lost 230 grams and was cleared for takeoff.
When the big day finally came, McGrath says she was rearing to go, squawking and wriggling until the very last moment.
"She was crazy," McGrath said. "She was literally bouncing in her crate."
Katherine McGrath, director of operations at the Southwest Virginia Wildlife Center, released the hawk on Friday outside a high school in Roanoke. (Submitted by Katherine McGrath)
McGrath says the chicken-owning neighbours have been warned of the hawk's release, and the bird has been tagged in case she ever gets herself in trouble again.
But while she admits she'll miss her feisty patient, McGrath says she hopes to "never see her again."
"It's always better for the animal to be free," she said.
'Internationally famous'
Dozens of people came out on Friday to watch the hawk take flight outside the local high school.

"They had seen her online. They were just in love with her story," McGrath said. "Roanoke, Virginia, isn't a big town. So having something go internationally famous here, you know it's something to show up for."
McGrath says the hawk didn't appreciate her brief stint in captivity, and that's a good thing. (Submitted by Katherine McGrath)

She says it's unlikely this experience has taught the bird a lesson about the dangers of overindulging on local, organic poultry. After all, she says, it's perfectly natural for a wild animal to gorge when it finds an abundance of food ahead of the long, lean winter.

But being caged, manhandled and put on a forced diet has probably taught her to deplore humans even more than she already did, which was quite a bit. While the wildlife staff loved her, McGrath says the feeling was decidedly not mutual.
"So, hopefully, she'll be a little more wary of people, which will help her stay away from those chickens," she said.
